blocks.text: A 35-year-old man attends a fertility clinic with his 32-year-old wife. They have been trying to conceive for two years. His wife's initial assessment has not identified an obvious cause.

items.text: Take a focused male reproductive history.
Explain the role of semen analysis.
Outline the investigations for suspected male factor infertility.

blocks.text: Alternative scenarios

items.text: A man with azoospermia on semen analysis.
A man with a history of undescended testes.
A patient with low sperm concentration and reduced motility.
A man who uses testosterone injections and wishes to father a child.
A couple seeking counselling about IVF and ICSI.

blocks.text: Male factor infertility refers to impaired male reproductive function that reduces the likelihood of conception. It may involve sperm production, sperm transport, ejaculation, sexual function or other reproductive factors.

rows: Problems affecting hormonal stimulation of sperm production
Impaired sperm production within the testes
Genetic disorders, undescended testes, testicular damage
Vas deferens obstruction, ejaculatory duct obstruction
Interference with intercourse or semen deposition
No single cause identified or multiple contributors

blocks.text: Important: Abnormal semen parameters do not automatically mean that natural conception is impossible. Likewise, a normal semen analysis does not guarantee fertility.
Start sensitively because fertility problems may cause embarrassment, anxiety or concerns about masculinity.

items.text: Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Explain why you need to discuss sexual and reproductive health.
Ask permission before discussing sensitive topics or examining the genitalia.
Offer a chaperone for an intimate examination according to local practice.

blocks.text: “Hello, my name is …, and I am one of the doctors in the fertility clinic. I understand that you and your partner have been trying to conceive without success. Male reproductive factors can sometimes contribute to this, and many causes can be investigated or treated. I would like to ask you some questions about your general health, previous illnesses, medications and reproductive health. Is that alright with you?”
Avoid phrases such as “You are infertile” before an appropriate assessment has been completed.
Use a systematic approach.

content_groups.group_title: A. Presenting complaint and reproductive history

items.text: How long have you and your partner been trying to conceive?
Have you fathered a pregnancy before?
Have you fathered a child with your current or a previous partner?
Have you undergone fertility investigations before?
Have you ever had a semen analysis?
Have you ever been told that your sperm count was low?
Have you had any previous fertility treatment?

blocks.text: Interpretation: Previous paternity does not exclude acquired infertility. New illness, surgery, medication use or age-related changes may affect reproductive function.

items.text: Ability to achieve and maintain an erection.
Use of lubricants, particularly products that may impair sperm motility.
Relationship stress or other barriers to intercourse.

blocks.text: Erectile dysfunction and ejaculatory disorders may prevent conception even when sperm production is normal.

items.text: Congenital abnormalities of the genital tract.

blocks.text: These histories may indicate impaired sperm production or obstruction of sperm transport.

items.text: Genital tuberculosis or sexually transmitted infections where relevant.
Previous pelvic, inguinal or scrotal surgery.

blocks.text: Clinical reasoning: Diabetes can contribute to erectile dysfunction and ejaculatory problems. Chemotherapy may impair spermatogenesis. Previous inguinal surgery can occasionally damage structures involved in sperm transport.
This is particularly important.

items.text: Opioids and other medications that may affect hormonal function.
Certain medications associated with sexual dysfunction.

blocks.text: High-yield OSCE point: Exogenous testosterone can suppress pituitary LH and FSH secretion, lowering intratesticular testosterone and potentially causing severe oligospermia or azoospermia. It should not be prescribed as fertility treatment in a man wishing to conceive.
Do not advise a patient to stop prescribed medication abruptly. Arrange a clinician-led review of possible reproductive effects.

items.text: Occupational contact with pesticides, solvents or other reproductive toxins.

blocks.text: A febrile illness may temporarily impair semen parameters, which is one reason an abnormal result may need repeating.

items.text: Cystic fibrosis or congenital absence of the vas deferens in the family.
Early menopause in female relatives, where relevant to a shared genetic assessment.

blocks.text: Explore the impact of infertility on self-esteem, relationships and mental well-being. Ask about the couple's expectations and treatment preferences.
Do not equate infertility with sexual inadequacy or lack of masculinity.
In an examination station, explain the procedure, obtain consent, offer a chaperone and ensure privacy.
Features of hypogonadism may include reduced facial hair, reduced muscle mass, decreased libido or gynaecomastia, although none is diagnostic on its own.
1. Penis
Inspect for anatomical abnormalities, hypospadias, phimosis or other conditions that may interfere with intercourse or semen deposition.
2. Testes
Assess testicular size, consistency, position, symmetry and tenderness. Small testes may suggest impaired spermatogenesis or hormonal dysfunction.
3. Epididymides and vas deferens
Assess for tenderness, masses and palpable vas deferens. Congenital absence of the vas deferens can be associated with obstructive azoospermia and CFTR-related genetic variants.
4. Spermatic cords and varicocele
Examine for dilated veins, typically more apparent when standing and during Valsalva manoeuvre. A palpable clinical varicocele may be relevant in a man with infertility and abnormal semen parameters.

content_groups.group_title: C. How to report the examination

blocks.text: Normal findings:

“On examination, the patient has normal male secondary sexual characteristics. The penis is anatomically normal. Both testes are descended, symmetrical and of normal size and consistency. The epididymides and vasa deferentia are palpable bilaterally. There is no palpable varicocele or testicular mass.”

items.text: “Both testes are small and soft, raising concern for impaired spermatogenesis or hypogonadism.”
“The right testis is absent from the scrotum, and an undescended testis must be considered.”
“The left spermatic cord has palpable dilated veins consistent with a clinical varicocele.”
“The vas deferens is not palpable bilaterally, raising suspicion of congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.”
“There is a firm intratesticular mass requiring urgent specialist assessment.”

blocks.text: A genital examination should be performed by a suitably trained clinician and interpreted alongside semen analysis and other investigations.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. Semen analysis: the most important investigation

blocks.text: Semen analysis is a first-line investigation in male infertility.

content_groups.group_title: A. How to collect a semen sample

items.text: Follow the laboratory's recommended abstinence period, commonly 2–7 days.
Collect the sample by masturbation into a clean, appropriate container.
Avoid ordinary lubricants or condoms unless the laboratory specifically provides a sperm-safe product.
Collect the entire ejaculate and report any spillage.
Label and transport the specimen according to the laboratory's timing and temperature instructions.
Provide details of recent fever or illness where requested.

blocks.text: If a sample is abnormal, repeat testing may be needed because semen parameters vary.

The following are the WHO 6th-edition lower fifth-percentile reference values from men whose partners conceived within 12 months. These are reference limits, not absolute boundaries between fertile and infertile men.
Interpret these values with the laboratory report, clinical history and the other semen parameters. A value below a reference limit does not by itself prove sterility.

rows: No sperm detected in the ejaculate
Reduced proportion of sperm with normal morphology
Reduced concentration, motility and normal morphology

blocks.text: Scenario 1: Oligozoospermia
Sperm concentration is 8 million/mL.
Interpretation: Reduced sperm concentration. Repeat semen analysis as indicated and assess for testicular, endocrine, genetic or other causes.
Scenario 2: Asthenozoospermia
Total sperm motility is 25%.
Interpretation: Reduced total motility relative to the WHO reference value. Review the complete report, sample quality, recent illness and possible male reproductive factors.
Scenario 3: Azoospermia
No sperm are seen in the ejaculate.
Interpretation: Confirm the finding according to laboratory protocol, including examination of a centrifuged sample when appropriate. Differentiate obstructive from non-obstructive causes.
Scenario 4: Low semen volume
Semen volume is 0.8 mL.
Interpretation: Consider incomplete collection, retrograde ejaculation, androgen deficiency or ejaculatory duct obstruction, depending on the clinical context.
Scenario 5: Abnormal morphology
Only 2% of sperm have normal morphology.
Interpretation: Below the lower reference value. Assess the complete semen profile; isolated morphology abnormalities do not independently establish infertility.

blocks.title: Problems with hormonal stimulation of the testes:

items.text: Suppression of LH and FSH by exogenous testosterone or anabolic steroids.
Some cases of varicocele-associated impaired spermatogenesis.
Congenital absence of the vas deferens.
Selected genital tract infections causing obstruction.
Anatomical abnormalities interfering with semen deposition.

blocks.text: Genetic investigations may be appropriate in selected cases of severe oligozoospermia or azoospermia.

items.text: CFTR-related variants associated with congenital absence of the vas deferens.

blocks.text: Testing depends on the semen findings, clinical history and current specialist guidelines.
Do not order every test for every patient. Investigations should follow the history, examination and semen analysis.

rows: Abnormal semen parameters, small testes or suspected hormonal dysfunction
Selected patients with low testosterone, low libido or suspected pituitary disease
Palpable mass, uncertain examination or selected structural concerns
Selected severe sperm-production disorders or suspected congenital abnormalities
Transrectal ultrasound or other targeted imaging
Selected cases of suspected ejaculatory duct obstruction
Congenital absence of the vas deferens or selected obstructive azoospermia cases
When clinical and biochemical findings suggest pituitary pathology

blocks.text: Important: Semen analysis is not a substitute for a clinical assessment, and imaging is not routinely required in every man with an abnormal semen result.
Management depends on the underlying cause, severity of the semen abnormality, female partner's age and reproductive status, and the couple's preferences.

items.text: Stop smoking and recreational drug use.
Avoid anabolic steroids and non-prescribed testosterone.
Review prescribed medications with the treating clinician.
Optimise weight, nutrition and chronic disease control.
Provide emotional support and realistic counselling.

blocks.text: Lifestyle modification can improve general health and sometimes semen parameters, but it is not a guaranteed treatment for infertility.
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
Specialist-directed gonadotrophin therapy or pulsatile GnRH in selected cases may stimulate spermatogenesis.
Exogenous testosterone-associated infertility
Review testosterone treatment with the prescribing clinician and refer for specialist management. Recovery may take months or longer; do not stop medication without appropriate medical guidance.
Obstructive azoospermia
Selected patients may benefit from microsurgical reconstruction or sperm retrieval followed by assisted reproduction.
Non-obstructive azoospermia
Investigate the cause and discuss specialist options, including selected sperm-retrieval procedures and assisted reproduction where appropriate.
Clinical varicocele
Consider repair in selected men with infertility, a palpable varicocele and abnormal semen parameters, taking account of the couple's reproductive circumstances.
Erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction
Treat the underlying cause and consider appropriate sexual medicine or urology referral. Assisted reproduction may be an option when natural semen deposition is not possible.

items.text: IUI: May be suitable in selected cases of mild male-factor infertility when the processed sperm count and other clinical factors are favourable.
IVF: May be considered according to the couple's overall fertility assessment.
ICSI: A single sperm is injected into an egg and may be appropriate for severe male-factor infertility, selected sperm-retrieval cases or previous fertilisation failure.
Surgical sperm retrieval: May be offered in selected cases of obstructive or non-obstructive azoospermia.

blocks.text: ICSI does not eliminate every fertility risk, and the underlying cause may have implications for offspring. Genetic counselling and testing should be discussed when indicated.

Arrange follow-up to review the semen analysis, hormonal or genetic investigations where appropriate, treatment options and the couple's preferences. Refer to a reproductive urologist or fertility specialist when indicated.
Q1. What is the first-line investigation for male infertility?
Answer: Semen analysis, interpreted with the clinical history and examination. Repeat testing may be needed when the initial result is abnormal.
Q2. What is azoospermia?
Answer: The absence of sperm in the ejaculate, confirmed according to appropriate laboratory procedures. The cause may be obstructive or non-obstructive.
Q3. Differentiate obstructive and non-obstructive azoospermia.

Answer: Obstructive azoospermia results from impaired sperm transport despite sperm production, whereas non-obstructive azoospermia results from severely impaired sperm production. Hormonal findings, testicular examination and targeted investigations help distinguish them.
Q4. Why does testosterone treatment impair fertility?
Answer: Exogenous testosterone suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH through negative feedback. This reduces intratesticular testosterone and may markedly suppress spermatogenesis.
Q5. What is a varicocele?
Answer: Dilatation of the pampiniform plexus veins in the spermatic cord. A palpable varicocele may be associated with impaired semen parameters in some men.
Q6. What is ICSI?
Answer: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection, a technique in which a single sperm is injected directly into an egg during IVF.
Q7. Does abnormal sperm morphology alone prove infertility?
Answer: No. Morphology is one parameter among several. It must be interpreted alongside sperm concentration, motility, the clinical history and the couple's overall reproductive assessment.
Q8. When would you request genetic testing?

Answer: In selected patients with azoospermia, severe oligozoospermia, congenital absence of the vas deferens or clinical features suggesting a genetic cause. The exact tests depend on current guidelines and the suspected diagnosis.

items.text: Forgetting to ask about testosterone or anabolic steroid use.
Interpreting a single semen analysis as definitive.
Confusing low sperm concentration with azoospermia.
Assuming a normal erection proves normal sperm production.
Ordering scrotal ultrasound routinely without a clinical indication.
Prescribing testosterone to a man actively seeking fertility.
Failing to consider genetic counselling in selected severe cases.
Discussing ICSI without explaining the overall fertility assessment and relevant risks.
